title: Hajar in the valley
hook: Ibrahim leaves Hajar and baby Isma'il in a dry valley, and she asks: did Allah command this? then we will not be lost
carry: then we will not be lost

segments.voice: Yesterday: guests with news, and a roasted calf set before strangers. Your line was hurry to the guest. Did someone get fed today before they had to ask? Day thirty-nine.

A valley with nothing in it. No trees. No well. No town. Rock on both sides, heat coming up off the ground. A man walks in with a woman and a baby, sets down a leather bag of dates and a skin of water, and turns to go. She gets up and follows him. Ibrahim, are you leaving us here, in a valley with no people and nothing in it? He doesn't answer. She asks again. He keeps walking, and he doesn't look back. What she asks next is short, and it isn't an accusation. Today: Hajar in the valley.
screen: `A VALLEY WITH NOTHING IN IT.` → `SHE FOLLOWS HIM.` → `HE DOESN'T LOOK BACK.`

segments.voice: This story isn't told in the Qur'an itself. It comes from a long hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated from Ibn Abbas. Hajar is the mother of Ibrahim's son Isma'il. Jews and Christians know her as Hagar, from Genesis. Here's the moment the hadith keeps. She follows Ibrahim, asking, and he won't answer. So she changes the question. Did Allah command you to do this? And he says yes. And she says, in effect: then He will not let us be lost. And she walks back to her baby. Notice what she did. She didn't stop asking. She found the one question that mattered, got her answer, and let it hold her. That's not the same as feeling fine. The dates and water are about to run out, and tomorrow we'll see what that costs her. But her trust is the ground she stands on while she runs. Then the hadith gives us Ibrahim's side. When he reached a place where they couldn't see him, he turned toward the valley, raised his hands and prayed. That prayer is in the Qur'an, in Surah Ibrahim. He says: our Lord, I have settled some of my children in a valley without crops, near Your sacred House, so that they may establish prayer. So make the hearts of people incline toward them, and provide them with fruits, that they may give thanks. He didn't look back at them. But he looked back at the valley, out of sight, and asked for everything they'd need. That empty valley is Mecca. Pilgrims now walk where she stood.
screen: `A HADITH FROM IBN ABBAS.` · `DID ALLAH COMMAND THIS?` · `HE WILL NOT LET US BE LOST.` · `A PRAYER FROM OUT OF SIGHT.` · then, large: `A VALLEY WITHOUT CROPS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: trust one thing you can't control. Settle, and breathe. Find the thing on your mind that you keep checking on. A test result. A child far away. Money. A decision someone else is making. Hold it for a moment. Notice whether your hands want to do something with it. Then, on a long breath out, set it down, the way Hajar walked back to the baby. It won't stop being real. You're just not carrying it alone for these two minutes. If you pray, you can hand it over by name. The bell holds the time.
Hajar in the valley. A mother left with a baby, a bag of dates and one question that gave her somewhere to stand. Today's word.
Your line: then we will not be lost. When the worry comes back today, and it will, ask Hajar's question once, and let it be enough for the next hour. Day thirty-nine.

screen: `DAY 39 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: SEVEN RUNS AND A SPRING.`

howItsDone: Muslims remember Hajar at Mecca, where the valley she was left in became the city around the Ka'ba; her trust is often retold in sermons on tawakkul, reliance on Allah.

match.prompt: who did what in the story — tap the pairs.
pairs: walked away and didn't look back
dates, and a skin of water
Ibrahim raised his hands and prayed

myth: the Qur'an tells the whole story of Hajar in the valley
the story comes from a hadith in Bukhari. the Qur'an gives Ibrahim's prayer for the valley, in Surah Ibrahim.
the empty valley in the story is where Mecca now stands
Ibrahim's prayer places it near the sacred House.
Hajar stopped asking questions and just accepted it
she kept asking, then changed the question: did Allah command this?

fork.setup: you're Hajar. Ibrahim is walking away, leaving you and the baby in an empty valley. he won't answer you. what do you ask?
options: how could you leave us here?
did Allah command you to do this?
fork.reveal: she asks if Allah commanded it. he says yes, and she says He will not let us be lost, and goes back to the baby.

original.note: Arabic, from Qur'an 14:37: "in a valley without crops," Ibrahim's words for the place he left them.

trapdoor: what you thought: a man abandons his family in the desert.
what it means: in the hadith, Hajar asks one question, whether Allah commanded it, and her trust becomes the ground she stands on.
what a scholar hears: the story is in Bukhari, from Ibn Abbas; the Qur'an holds only Ibrahim's prayer from out of sight, in Surah Ibrahim 14:37.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 3364 (Hajar and Isma'il left in the valley, narrated from Ibn Abbas)
Genesis 16 and 21 (Hagar, named as a neighbor)

notes: Hadith number (Bukhari 3364) cited from memory; please confirm, and confirm the paraphrase of Hajar's words ("then He will not neglect / let us be lost").

"Hajar was Ibrahim's second wife": Muslim scholars generally describe her as his wife; some accounts describe her first as Sarah's servant. Stated simply as second wife; a Keeper may prefer different wording.
14:37 paraphrased, not quoted. The script places the prayer 'out of sight' following the hadith's sequence.
"Millions of people now walk where she stood" refers to pilgrims in Mecca; general statement.
The index hook references (14:37; Bukhari); kept.
